newsitem.title: UK: Single currency could divide EU, Britain says.
newsitem.headline: Single currency could divide EU, Britain says.

text.p: Britain voiced new doubts on Wednesday about the pace of integration in the European Union, saying a single currency could split the bloc and entail massive consequences for the EU's decision-making processes.

In a speech prepared for delivery at Zurich University, Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind rejected "the ratchet of unending institutional integration" and appealed instead for Europe to develop as a partnership of nations.

"We should not proceed down a path of integration faster or further than our people are prepared to go," Rifkind said. Britain' ruling Conservative party is deeply split over the question of closer ties with the EU.
Britain was committed to Europe and would not turn its back on it, Rifkind said. But the EU could not be treated as "an experiment in a sanitised political laboratory," he added.

"A political entity can only grow organically, as a natural expression of a common identity and of common aims. You cannot superimpose those things, nor force the pace, without encountering resistance," he said.
Rifkind said closer cooperation by groups of nations in areas such as defence and immigration controls was sensible and would become unavoidable in an enlarged EU of 20 or 25 states.
But he said it was important to get the flexibility right to maintain the bloc's cohesion.

If a single currency went ahead, the EU would be divided into two groups of members for the foreseeable future because around half of the existing 15 members and virtually all 12 applicants would not meet the eligibility criteria.
A senior British official said Rifkind was worried about the broader institutional implications of the single currency.

If, for example, half of the EU had opted out of core commitments such as the common agricultural policy or the single market, the bloc's decision-making processes would doubtlessly have been very different, the official argued.
Rifkind was making his speech to mark the 50th anniversary of a call by British wartime prime minister Winston Churchill for the setting up of "a kind of United States of Europe".

Rifkind said Britain had other goals -- strengthening European defence cooperation, increasing the continent's industrial competitiveness, using the EU's muscle to press for global free trade, and bringing prosperity to eastern Europe.

"It is a vision based on choosing carefully the stepping stones toward closer cooperation; not jumping blindly toward ever greater integration, flailing for footholds that may prove precarious or illusory," he said.
"We believe Europe will thrive as a partnership of nations... we believe in incremental progress and not in leaps of faith," he said.
Rifkind called for a sense of realism in the current intergovernmental conference to reshape the EU's institutions.

"We all want to avert future tragedies like Bosnia," he said. "Improving the workings of the common foreign and security policy could help do that. But can anyone really believe more lives would have been saved in Bosnia, or peace have come sooner, if the EU had taken votes by qualified majority?"
